title: Why we start engineering in week five
ex: Waiting for every screen to be finished before writing code is how projects slip. Here's how the overlap actually works.
author: tomas
body:
The classic agency plan is a waterfall with nicer fonts: design everything, get sign-off, then build everything. It looks tidy on a Gantt chart and it fails the same way every time. Design runs long because nobody wants to sign off a screen they haven't seen working, and engineering starts late, discovers the awkward parts, and sends the screens back.

The overlap

On a Gevix project, engineering starts in week five, when design is roughly a third done. By then the core flow has been tested with users and the data model is stable, which is all a build actually needs to begin. The remaining screens (settings, edge cases, admin) get designed while the first ones are being built.

That means the engineer sees the design as it forms, and the designer sees the build as it forms. Problems surface in a Slack thread on a Tuesday instead of a review meeting in week ten.

What it needs

  • A written scope, signed in week two, so both disciplines agree on what "done" means.
  • One shared Figma file and one repository, with everyone in both.
  • A Friday demo on a staging URL, every week, from week six onwards.
Design and engineering aren't phases. They're two people looking at the same problem from different chairs.

It's not a trick to go faster, although projects do finish sooner. It's that the product is better when the two halves of the team argue early and often.

title: The handoff problem, and how we avoid it
ex: Most products get worse the moment a designer hands over a file. We stopped handing over.
author: mara
body:
Every product designer has watched it happen. You spend six weeks on a flow, hand over the file, and three weeks later the build comes back subtly wrong. The spacing is off, the empty state is missing, and a dropdown has become a modal for reasons nobody can explain.

Nobody was careless. Handoff is just lossy. A Figma file can't hold intent, and a spec document can't cover every case, so the engineer fills the gaps with guesses.

Our fix is boring

We stopped handing over. The designer on a project stays on it through the build, reviews pull requests (yes, actual pull requests) and answers questions in the thread where they come up. The engineer is in the Figma file from week one, commenting on what will be hard before it gets polished.

What changes

  • Empty states, errors and loading states get designed, because the engineer asks for them.
  • Components get built once and reused, because the designer can see the codebase.
  • The "final" screen is the one in the browser, not the one in Figma.

If you already have an engineering team, we still won't hand over a folder of PNGs. We build the component library in your codebase alongside them, and the spec comes with it.

title: React Native in 2026: when we still go native
ex: One codebase for both stores is the default. These are the four cases where we don't.
author: jonas
body:
Most mobile apps we build are React Native. One codebase, both stores, a team that can move between web and mobile. In 2026 the framework is mature enough that "is it good enough?" isn't really a question any more.

But we still go native, in Swift and Kotlin, for a minority of projects. Here are the cases.

When we go native

  • Hardware is the product. Bluetooth peripherals, camera pipelines, background sensor logging. The bridges exist, but you end up writing native code anyway, so start there.
  • Platform features on day one. Widgets, Live Activities, App Clips, watch apps. React Native gets these eventually; native gets them at launch.
  • Heavy animation and gesture work. Reanimated is excellent. A physics-driven, interruptible interaction is still easier to get right natively.
  • An existing native team. If your engineers write Swift, we write Swift.

When we don't

Everything else: forms, lists, maps, payments, chat, dashboards. Northloop is a good example. Ride tracking, Strava import, coach chat and a training plan, all from one codebase, with both stores updated on the same afternoon.

The question isn't "which is better". It's "what does this app spend its time doing".

title: Pricing pages are product design
ex: The upgrade flow is the most-read screen you'll ever ship. Treat it like one.
author: ada
body:
Ask a SaaS founder to list their product's screens and the pricing page rarely makes the list. It's marketing, it lives on the website, someone will sort it out before launch.

It's also the most-read screen you'll ship. Every prospect reads it, most of them twice, and it's where they decide whether the product is for them.

Design it like a product screen

  • Name plans by who they're for, not by adjectives. "For a team of five" beats "Pro".
  • Show the one number that drives cost. Seats, projects, invoices. If your pricing has three variables, your prospect has a spreadsheet open.
  • Put the upgrade path in the app. The moment someone hits a limit is the moment they'll pay. A dead-end error is a lost upgrade.
  • Test it with real users. We put the pricing page in front of five people in the same session as the onboarding flow.

Ledgerly

On Ledgerly we redesigned the pricing page twice before launch, and the upgrade prompt inside the app three times. The final version is the one that stopped generating support tickets asking what the difference between the plans was.

title: What a two-week design sprint actually produces
ex: A prototype, five user sessions, and a build estimate you can take to your board.
author: mara
body:
"Design sprint" has become a vague term. Here's precisely what ours produces in two weeks, so you can decide whether it's worth it.

Week one

Monday and Tuesday are interviews: your team, then five people who'd use the product. Wednesday we map the core flow on a wall (or a FigJam board). Thursday and Friday are sketching, in low fidelity, on purpose.

Week two

Monday to Wednesday we build a clickable prototype of the one flow that matters most. Thursday we test it with five users, recorded. Friday we write up what happened and what we'd change.

What you leave with

  • A Figma prototype you can put in front of investors or your board.
  • Five recorded user sessions and a two-page summary.
  • A build estimate for a first version, in weeks and cost, with the assumptions written down.
  • An honest answer on whether to build it at all.
About one sprint in four ends with "don't build this yet". That's the sprint paying for itself.

title: Fast marketing sites without a build team
ex: How we set up Framer so a two-person marketing team ships pages weekly.
author: ada
body:
A marketing site has one job: let a small team publish quickly without breaking anything. Most of the sites we inherit fail at that. A new page needs an engineer, so new pages don't get made.

Why Framer

For most studios and startups we build the marketing site in Framer. Designers work directly in it, the CMS is built in, hosting and forms are handled, and the output is fast without tuning. Halden Studio's site has sixty case studies and a journal, and the partners publish both themselves.

How we set it up

  • A component library with the ten or so blocks the team actually needs. Not forty.
  • CMS collections with sensible required fields, so a post can't go out without an image.
  • Performance budgets: every page under a second on 4G, checked before handover.
  • A one-hour recorded walkthrough, so the next hire can learn it too.

When we use Next.js instead

If the site shares components with a product, needs authentication, or pulls live data, it's Next.js. Same design system, more moving parts.

title: Thirty days after launch: what breaks
ex: The bugs that only real users find, and why we keep the team on for a month.
author: jonas
body:
Launch day is calm. The week after is when the real bugs arrive, because real people do things test users never did. Every fixed-scope project includes thirty days of fixes, and this is what those thirty days usually contain.

What actually breaks

  • Data nobody imagined. A client name with 400 characters. A ride with zero distance. An invoice for a negative amount.
  • Old devices. The phone that's three OS versions behind and belongs to your biggest customer.
  • Email. Password resets in spam, receipts with the wrong timezone, a template that looks fine everywhere except Outlook.
  • The thing that worked on staging. Usually an environment variable.

How we run the month

Monitoring is on from day one (Sentry for errors, PostHog for behaviour), and the same team that built the product is on call for it. We triage every morning, fix the same day where we can, and ship a summary each Friday.

By day thirty the error rate has usually flattened, and the conversation shifts from fixes to what's next. That's when most clients move to a monthly team.

title: The SEO work that's just good engineering
ex: Most of what moves rankings on a new site is markup, speed and structure. Here's the checklist we ship with.
author: tomas
body:
There's a version of SEO that's tricks: keyword stuffing, link schemes, content farms. We don't do that. There's another version that's mostly just building the site properly, and we do that on every project whether or not anyone says "SEO".

The checklist we ship with

  • Semantic markup: one h1 per page, real headings, landmarks, lists that are lists.
  • Core Web Vitals in the green: largest paint under 2.5 seconds, no layout shift, inputs that respond.
  • Meta descriptions and Open Graph tags written by a person, per page.
  • Structured data where it applies: organisation, articles, products, FAQs.
  • A sitemap, sensible URLs, and redirects for every old URL when we replace a site.
  • Images with real alt text, sized and lazy-loaded.

What's separate

Keyword research, a content plan, and monthly work on rankings are a different job with a different rhythm. We offer it as a monthly engagement, usually paired with a writer on your side.

Good rankings on a new site are mostly a side effect of a site that's fast, clear and correct.
